column2: Name the adult who accepts care, and require a reply before the first adult leaves.
column3: Say, “Maya, you have Leo now.” Maya replies, “I have Leo.” Both check Leo against the attendance list.

column2: Teach a workable bathroom plan for each setting; an unavailable helper is not an answer.
column3: Keep the children with an approved caregiver while another helps in the bathroom. A provider working alone needs a safe plan that works without a second adult.

column2: Explain why counting heads cannot replace matching each child to the live list.
column3: Check each child's name and face against today's arrivals and departures. Ten children on the list and ten in the room do not prove they are the same ten.

column2: Give a practical way to pause deliveries and conversations while keeping children in view.
column3: Ask the delivery person to wait. Keep watching the children and speak with one arriving family at a time.

column2: Supply ages, attendance, qualified staff, license category, and the cited limit before asking for a legal admission decision.
column3: Check the children who would actually attend, their ages, the qualified adults, and the license limits before promising the extra day.

column2: Distinguish a birthday from a legally permitted staffing transition.
column3: Do not reduce staff just because a birthday occurred. Check the age definition and any transition conditions in the applicable rule.

column2: Identify household and related children explicitly; exemptions must be cited.
column3: Put the caregiver's own child on the planning list, then check whether that child counts under the applicable rule. Being related does not answer the question.

column2: Ask the learner to check the combined group's ages and approved room, not just total attendance.
column3: Before joining groups, check the combined ages, qualified adults, group limit, and room approval. A quiet closing period still needs a valid plan.

column2: Separate clearance, supervised provisional work, unsupervised care, and counting in staffing.
column3: Do not assume a substitute may supervise children or count as staff while clearance is unresolved. Check the exact role permitted by the applicable rule.

column2: List the director requirements and evidence; experience alone is not a legal qualification.
column3: Check the documents needed for the director role before changing the person's duties. Years as an assistant do not settle whether those requirements are met.

column2: State which volunteer duties are proposed and whether the person may count in staffing.
column3: A volunteer can help only within an allowed role. Do not count an extra pair of hands as a qualified caregiver without checking.

column2: Teach credential verification without promising interstate recognition.
column3: Ask the issuing body and the local licensing authority what the credential covers. Keep written confirmation of any additional requirements.

column2: Identify the exact expired qualification and the coverage consequence.
column3: Check who still has the needed valid training and change the schedule if necessary. Book the required renewal; do not alter the old certificate.

column2: Provide acceptance criteria for the course, delivery format, and assessment.
column3: Match the course to the authority's accepted training requirements. A printed certificate by itself does not show the course is accepted.

column2: Use a real break schedule and identify who remains qualified on site.
column3: Before a break starts, name the qualified person covering the group. If no eligible cover is available, change the schedule rather than leave a gap.

column2: Use a teach-back task tied to an actual emergency role.
column3: Ask the new worker to show the exit route, find the attendance list, and explain their assigned emergency job before working independently.

column2: Replace a vague hazard answer with explicit safe-sleep teaching; cite authoritative guidance and state exceptions separately.
column3: For the teaching example, remove the stuffed toy from the infant's sleep space. Explain that a familiar toy from home does not make a sleep space safe. Verify final safe-sleep wording against current sources.

column2: Name the non-sleep equipment, the safe transfer action, and trained emergency response if needed.
column3: In the example, a baby falls asleep in a swing. Move the baby safely to an appropriate infant sleep space; do not keep the swing as the routine sleep place. Verify current clinical and licensing guidance.

column2: Avoid inventing a universal observation interval; explain the limits of a monitor.
column3: A monitor can miss a blocked view or a disconnected device. Follow the required direct checks and keep the record required for that license category.

column2: Do not imply that a parent's request creates a safe-sleep exception.
column3: Listen to the parent's concern, explain the safe-sleep procedure, and check any legally permitted medical exception through the proper process. Parent preference alone is not approval.

column2: Separate routine medication consent from time-critical emergency medication.
column3: For a routine medicine request, check the required written authorization, child, label, dose, time, route, and trained person. Do not use this routine checklist to delay an emergency response under the child's plan.

column2: Teach identity checks at administration, not recognition of the bottle's color.
column3: Read the child's name and instructions on the actual container and check the record before giving medicine. Two similar bottles need separate, clear storage.

column2: Specify no duplicate dose, clinical advice, and emergency escalation without giving dosing advice.
column3: Do not give another dose to fill a blank record. Keep the child supervised and contact the qualified clinical advice route in the medication plan; use emergency services for urgent symptoms.

column2: Distinguish a readiness drill from an active allergic or medical emergency.
column3: During a check, find the child's emergency medicine and confirm who can use it. During an actual emergency, follow the child's emergency plan and summon emergency help without delaying for paperwork.

column2: Explain uncertain ingredients and cross-contact; do not teach that removing visible nuts makes food safe.
column3: Do not serve the unlabeled snack to the child whose allergy plan requires ingredient checks. Offer a food already checked against that plan.

column2: Teach that changing utensils alone may not fix contaminated food.
column3: Stop using the shared utensil. Set aside food affected by cross-contact, use clean equipment, and prepare a suitable replacement under the allergy plan.

column2: Give food type, elapsed time, and measured temperatures for any test requiring a safety decision.
column3: Keep the food out of service while checking reliable time and temperature information. Smell or appearance cannot establish that food is safe.

column2: Make the handoff reach the person preparing and serving the actual meal.
column3: Update the child's meal instructions and ask the serving adult to repeat the change. A message in an unread inbox does not protect the child at lunch.

column2: Separate ordinary exclusion decisions from emergency warning signs and disability accommodations.
column3: Observe how the child feels and whether they can take part safely. Use the applicable illness criteria and arrange urgent help for emergency signs; do not diagnose from a practice question.

column2: Teach caring supervision while arranging pickup; isolation must not mean abandonment.
column3: Keep the ill child comfortably supervised, arrange care for the rest of the group, and contact the family under the illness plan. Do not leave the child alone in a separate room.

column2: Explain the relationship between provider advice, public-health criteria, and licensing rules.
column3: Read what the return message actually says and compare it with applicable return criteria. Ask for clarification rather than treating an unclear note as automatic clearance.

column2: Add separate public-health and licensing notification checks and protect family privacy.
column3: Record the symptoms and dates without guessing a diagnosis. Contact the appropriate health authority for guidance and check licensing notice duties separately.

column2: Make “never leave a child on a changing surface” an explicit teaching point.
column3: Gather supplies before starting. If something is missing, keep the child safely attended and use a safe alternative; do not walk away from the changing surface.

column2: Teach handwashing as an action, with current CDC instructions to be cited.
column3: After toileting help, complete the required handwashing steps before preparing food. Wearing gloves does not remove the need for hand hygiene.

column2: Differentiate cleaning, sanitizing, and disinfecting; identify prohibited shared uses.
column3: Do not turn a diapering area into a food surface just by wiping it. Check permitted uses and follow the correct treatment steps for that surface.

column2: Use privacy that preserves required supervision; do not treat dignity as optional.
column3: Use a layout that shields the child from unnecessary viewing while the caregiver can still provide the required safe supervision and help.

column2: Do not invite smell-testing, relabeling by guess, or use of an unidentified chemical.
column3: Take the unmarked bottle out of use and secure it away from children. Do not sniff it or guess the contents; follow the approved identification or disposal process.

column2: Make the no-mixing action immediate; include exposure escalation rather than just policy review.
column3: Do not mix cleaning products. If products were mixed, keep children away and follow the exposure and emergency procedure; do not try another chemical to cancel the mixture.

column2: Explain wet contact time and label directions without inventing a universal duration.
column3: Read the product label and keep the surface wet for the specified time. A quick wipe may not complete the intended treatment.

column2: Teach secure storage and immediate action for a possible exposure.
column3: Move children away from the products and secure the supplies. If exposure may have occurred, use the appropriate poison or emergency advice route promptly.

column2: Distinguish a routine blocked-route discovery from a fire already in progress.
column3: During routine care, arrange safe supervision and clear the route safely. During a fire, use a safe evacuation route and the emergency plan rather than stay behind to move furniture.

column2: Test a backup contact method without making a practice call to an emergency line.
column3: Ask families to confirm contact details through the program's normal process. Test the backup communication system using an agreed non-emergency contact.

column2: Match supplies to infants, disabilities, medication access, and communication needs.
column3: Check whether the emergency kit works for the children present today. A kit packed before a new child enrolled may miss that child's needs.

column2: Teach one communicated reunification plan plus verified release.
column3: Use the plan's designated meeting place and communicate changes through the agreed channel. Confirm each child's authorized pickup before release.

column2: Do not infer accidental injury or abuse from an unexplained mark; assess both care and reporting needs.
column3: Record where the mark is and when it was noticed. Get appropriate care, preserve the child's exact words if offered, and assess reporting duties without inventing a cause.

column2: Separate parent notice, licensing notice, protective reporting, and emergency response.
column3: Identify each required recipient and deadline from the applicable rule. A call to the parent does not automatically satisfy a licensing or protective-reporting duty.

column2: Avoid implying every near-miss legally requires the same report.
column3: Remove the hazard and record what nearly happened for learning. Separately check whether this event meets any mandatory reporting rule.

column2: Explain when evidence collection must yield to emergency or protective reporting duties.
column3: Write each witness's own account separately and record what is unknown. Do not postpone needed care or a required report until everyone agrees.

column2: Teach calm listening, no promise of secrecy, no leading questions, and timely required reporting.
column3: Listen calmly. Do not promise secrecy or question the child to prove what happened. Record the child's own words and use the required reporting route; seek emergency help for immediate danger.

column2: Explicitly state that a supervisor's permission cannot substitute for the worker's own reporting obligation.
column3: Do not wait for the owner's approval when your reporting duty is triggered. Make the required report through the official route and follow internal notice steps without delaying it.

column2: Distinguish privacy from withholding information from authorized protective authorities.
column3: Do not discuss the concern in a staff chat or with unrelated families. Share necessary information with the authorized reporting and safety recipients.

column2: Do not require proof or an internal investigation before reporting a triggered concern.
column3: Use the official reporting authority to clarify uncertainty promptly. Do not collect proof first or let consultation delay a report already required by the applicable law.

column2: Replace abstract discipline language with an example of respectful guidance.
column3: Stop the humiliating response. Say, “I will help you keep everyone safe,” then guide the child toward a safe action instead of shaming them.

column2: Add developmental context, adult support, and an example of changing the environment.
column3: Separate children safely when needed. Reduce crowding by sending a small group to wash hands while the others do a short activity with adequate supervision.

column2: Do not teach restraint techniques; distinguish emergency protection from punishment.
column3: Move other children out of danger and use the least risky response within training and the applicable rules. Do not use physical control as punishment or teach a restraint from this workbook.

column2: Give an observable replacement for a value judgment.
column3: Replace “Ava was bad” with “Ava pushed a block toward Sam after Sam took the truck; the adult moved closer and helped them take turns.”

column2: Separate general inclusion duties from Head Start-specific suspension and expulsion rules.
column3: Address the immediate safety concern, then review individual supports, family input, and the rules that apply to this program before deciding on enrollment.

column2: Teach an individual accommodation discussion, not a blanket promise or refusal.
column3: Ask what support the child needs and consider a workable change. For example, offer an accessible path to the activity instead of saying all children must use the same route.

column2: Name need-to-know staff, readiness, and authorized access to the plan.
column3: Before a worker takes over, give them the child's necessary care instructions and have them explain what they will do. Keep unrelated private details restricted.

column2: Treat repeated early pickups as a possible exclusion pattern requiring review.
column3: Review why the child is repeatedly sent home, the support tried, and family input. Do not hide an enrollment restriction by calling every early pickup a one-time favor.

column2: Teach both identity and current release authority; familiarity or ID alone is insufficient.
column3: Keep the child supervised while checking the adult's identity and current pickup authorization. A driver's license identifies the adult but does not prove permission to collect this child.

column2: Require actual departure evidence; do not enter a convenient invented time.
column3: Check reliable departure information and make a dated correction that preserves the original entry. If the exact time is unknown, record that uncertainty.

column2: Do not interpret custody orders beyond competence or assume the pickup list overrides legal rights.
column3: Keep the child safe while the designated lead verifies current court documents and applicable release requirements. Seek authorized legal or agency help rather than guess who has legal custody.

column2: Teach continuing supervision and a real escalation plan; no unattended child or unapproved ride home.
column3: Stay with the child under safe supervision, try the authorized contacts, and follow the late-pickup escalation plan. Do not leave the child alone because closing time has passed.

column2: Make vehicle movement wait for a child-by-child reconciliation.
column3: Do not start the trip while the passenger list is wrong. Match each child to the correct vehicle list and resolve the mismatch first.

column2: Explain a physical vehicle check and any separately required verification.
column3: Check every row and space where a child could remain, following the transport procedure. A quiet vehicle or an unchecked box is not evidence that it is empty.

column2: Separate manufacturer fit and installation instructions from state legal minimums.
column3: Check the child's size, the restraint instructions, and vehicle instructions before travel. Do not guess from the child's age alone; verify the applicable transport law as well.

column2: Supply the driver's proposed role, vehicle category, and required documentation.
column3: Check the substitute's required driving, screening, training, and authorization records before departure. Being able to drive a personal car does not settle eligibility for this trip.

column2: Use effective physical separation of a hazard, not a verbal reminder alone.
column3: Block access to the damaged equipment and offer a safe play area. Reopen only after the repair and required safety checks are completed.

column2: Teach use of current alerts and named indoor alternatives, not unsupported universal cutoffs.
column3: Check current weather alerts and the program's applicable plan. Move the planned game indoors if the conditions call for it; yesterday's forecast is not enough.

column2: Distinguish water activity types, access barriers, rescue readiness, and supervision.
column3: Keep children away from the water until the specific activity has a safe, permitted plan. A decorative pond still presents a water-access risk.

column2: Require review before a destination changes; keep the original safe plan if verification is missing.
column3: Do not use the new destination until permissions, access, hazards, staffing, and transport are checked. A nearby location is not automatically covered by the old plan.

column2: Name anti-tip protection and keep children away during correction.
column3: Move children away from the unstable shelf. Have it properly secured or removed before children use the area again.

column2: Teach specific operational consequences instead of automatic closure or automatic continuation.
column3: Check whether drinking water, handwashing, toileting, temperature, and emergency communication can remain safe. Use the applicable contingency and closure requirements for the actual outage.

column2: Separate available floor space from licensed usable space.
column3: Do not begin care in the extra room until its required approval and safety checks are confirmed. An empty room is not automatically approved child-care space.

column2: Add dust, tool, access, and older-building exposure considerations without asserting a universal testing rule.
column3: Keep children out of the work area and control dust, tools, and entry routes. Check any applicable building or environmental requirements before work or reopening.

column2: Distinguish a visitor from a household member and an eligible caregiver.
column3: Keep the visitor within the permitted access arrangements while maintaining supervision. Visiting the home does not authorize them to take over child care.

column2: Identify who counts as a household member and any age-specific checks or notice deadlines.
column3: Before assuming no action is needed, check the rules for the new resident's age and access. Record required screening and notifications without inventing a deadline.

column2: Include animal health, handling, hand hygiene, and child-specific risks.
column3: Keep the animal separate until the activity has been checked. Plan safe handling, supervision, and handwashing, and account for the children's individual needs.

column2: Identify the actual hazard: weapons, chemicals, and choking items require different controls.
column3: Move children away and secure the item using the correct method for that hazard. Do not leave a dangerous object on a high but reachable shelf and call it secure.

column2: Separate recommended individual accounts from a claimed universal legal software requirement.
column3: Where the record system supports it, use each worker's own authorized login so entries can be traced. Check the actual privacy and record rules rather than assuming one software design is mandated everywhere.

column2: Define the specific use, audience, and consent scope; do not promise consent can override all restrictions.
column3: Do not post the photo under permission meant only for a private family update. Check the proposed use and any additional legal or program limits before sharing.

column2: Name the missing document; do not apply one admission decision to every missing form.
column3: Identify what is missing and whether it affects safe or lawful attendance. An emergency contact gap and a missing optional survey need different responses.

column2: Teach that retention periods depend on record type and that a hold may prevent deletion.
column3: Check the retention rule for that specific record and any legal hold before disposal. Do not delete all old files just because a cupboard is full.

column2: Avoid equating every attendance mismatch with fraud or assuming attendance-only reimbursement.
column3: Keep the original attendance and payment records, identify why they differ, and use the program's correction process. A mismatch needs review; it does not by itself prove fraud.

column2: Check effective payment periods and authorization terms instead of silently rewriting prior claims.
column3: Match the authorization change to its effective dates and the billing period. Correct a claim through the approved process rather than overwrite history.

column2: Account for program-specific enrollment and absence-payment rules; do not teach an attendance-only universal rule.
column3: Read this program's current payment terms before deciding whether an absence is payable. Another provider's experience or another state's rule is not enough.

column2: Identify allowed fees, copayments, exemptions, and current family obligations.
column3: Check which family charges this program allows and give the family a clear explanation of verified charges. Do not add an unsupported fee to make up a payment gap.

column2: Distinguish ownership transfer from a simple contact change; identify preapproval conditions.
column3: Check required licensing approval and notice before relying on the old license under new ownership. Do not assume a business sale transfers permission to operate.

column2: Teach proof that a correction works, with follow-up in ordinary operation.
column3: If a latch was repaired, test that it closes and secures properly during normal use. Keep the repair evidence and required submission; an invoice alone does not prove the hazard is fixed.

column2: Verify through an official contact while avoiding obstruction of lawful inspection.
column3: Follow the official identity-check procedure promptly and arrange lawful access. Do not invent a manager-only rule that blocks an authorized inspection.

column2: Explain source conflicts without teaching that a license condition overrides every higher law.
column3: Read the applicable rule and the actual license condition together. Ask the issuing authority to resolve an apparent conflict; do not assume a general handout cancels a specific restriction.

column2: Distinguish infant safe sleep from preschool rest and teach a respectful alternative.
column3: For a preschooler who is awake, consider an allowed quiet activity while others rest. Do not transfer a preschool rest example to an infant's sleep requirements.

column2: Teach plain language and checking understanding without shaming the reader or family.
column3: Use short sentences, pictures, or appropriate language support. Ask, “Can you tell me the pickup plan in your own words?” so unclear instructions can be fixed.

column2: Make learning participation concrete and preserve the same meaningful goal.
column3: If a child cannot grip a thin paintbrush, consider a larger handle or another accessible tool so the child can join the painting activity.

column2: Add learning goals, child observation, flexible routines, and actual implementation.
column3: Compare the written routine with what children experience. Adjust the plan or daily practice so the learning goal is meaningful and the actual requirements are met.

column2: Teach version control without destroying records that must be kept.
column3: Label the current policy, remove outdated working copies from daily use, and keep historical copies where required. Ask staff to explain the changed step.

column2: Give a measurable change and an observation of whether it worked.
column3: If children repeatedly reach a delivery doorway, change the handoff arrangement and check the next several deliveries. Another reminder alone does not test the fix.

column2: Separate the missed task from the late entry; do not teach that a late checklist cures an earlier failure.
column3: Record when the task was actually done and when the missed step was discovered. Address any remaining risk; a truthful late entry does not make an undone check timely.

column2: Teach proposed versus effective rules and source-change monitoring.
column3: Find the issuing authority's effective text and check its date and scope before changing practice. Keep the social media post as a lead, not as the rule.
